summary: Specifies how OSPFv2 routing extensions meet the routing requirements of the ITU-T Automatically Switched Optical Network architecture, working with the GMPLS control plane for optical transport networks.

plainLanguage.summary:
An optical network built to the ITU-T ASON design is split into routing areas stacked in a hierarchy, and a single router often stands for several separate optical nodes at once. OSPF's traffic engineering extensions had no way to say either of those things.

This RFC adds four small fields to the traffic engineering advertisements. Two name the optical node that a link or a set of address prefixes belongs to. Two record whether the information has already been passed up or down the hierarchy, so that it is not passed back to where it came from.

questions: what is ason routing for gmpls
how does ospfv2 support optical networks
what is a routing area in ason
what is the inter-ra export sub-tlv
subtitle: OSPFv2 extensions that let optical transport networks advertise their reachability and links, level by level.

tldr.problem: The ITU-T ASON architecture partitions the transport plane into routing areas arranged in a hierarchy, and one routing controller may speak for several transport nodes. Plain OSPFv2 traffic engineering extensions cannot express either of those things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds sub-TLVs to the OSPFv2 traffic engineering LSA: one naming the transport nodes at each end of a link, one tying advertised address prefixes to a transport node, and two marking whether routing information has already been exported up or down the hierarchy.
tldr.outcome: A router can advertise reachability and link topology on behalf of several transport nodes at once, and a hierarchy of routing areas can be built out of separate OSPF instances without routing information looping back. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5787.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Generalized Multiprotocol Label Switching protocol suite is designed to provide a control plane for a range of network technologies. These include optical networks such as time division multiplexing networks including SONET/SDH, Optical Transport Networks, and lambda switching optical networks.

The ITU-T defines the architecture of the Automatically Switched Optical Network in Recommendation G.8080. RFC 4258 describes the routing requirements for the GMPLS suite of routing protocols to support the capabilities and functionality of ASON control planes, and RFC 4652 evaluates the IETF link state routing protocols against those requirements. Section 7.1 of RFC 4652 summarizes the capabilities to be provided by OSPFv2 in support of ASON routing, and this document describes the OSPFv2 specifics.

Multi-layer transport networks are constructed from multiple networks of different technologies operating in a client-server relationship. The ASON routing model includes the definition of routing levels that provide scaling and confidentiality benefits. In multi-level routing, domains called routing areas are arranged in a hierarchical relationship. There is no implied relationship between multi-layer transport networks and multi-level routing, and the mechanisms described in the document work for both single-layer and multi-layer networks.

The work is scoped to the requirements and evaluation expressed in RFC 4258 and RFC 4652 and the ITU-T Recommendations that were current when those documents were written. Future extensions or revisions may be necessary if the ITU-T Recommendations are revised or if new requirements are introduced into a revision of RFC 4258.
sections.plainLanguage: GMPLS gives optical networks a control plane, and ASON says how that control plane should be organised. This document is the part that says how OSPF carries the extra information ASON needs.

sections.title: Routing Areas, OSPF Areas and Protocol Instances
sections.content:
An ASON routing area represents a partition of the transport plane, and its identifier is used within the control plane as the representation of this partition.

Routing areas are hierarchically contained: a higher-level, parent, RA contains lower-level, child, RAs that in turn may also contain RAs, so that RAs recursively define successive hierarchical levels. Routing information may be exchanged between levels of the RA hierarchy. The links connecting RAs may be viewed as external links, inter-RA links, and the links representing connectivity within an RA may be viewed as internal links, intra-RA links. The external links to an RA at one level of the hierarchy may be internal links in the parent RA, and intra-RA links of a child RA may be hidden from the parent RA's view.

An ASON routing area can be mapped to an OSPF area, but the hierarchy of ASON RA levels does not map to the hierarchy of OSPF areas. Instead, successive hierarchical levels of RAs must be represented by separate instances of the protocol, so that inter-level routing information exchange involves the export and import of routing information between protocol instances.

An ASON RA may therefore be identified by the combination of its OSPF Instance ID and its OSPF Area ID. With proper and careful network-wide configuration this can be achieved using just the OSPF Area ID, and the document recommends that process.
sections.plainLanguage: An RA is a piece of the optical network. RAs are nested, so a big area contains smaller ones. OSPF areas cannot be nested that way, so each level of the ASON hierarchy gets its own OSPF instance, and information passes between them.

sections.title: Terminology and Identification
sections.content:
There are three categories of identifiers used for ASON routing: transport-plane names, control-plane identifiers for components, and Signaling Communications Network addresses. GMPLS supports the separation of these identifiers and planes.

In the context of OSPF traffic engineering, an ASON transport node corresponds to a unique OSPF TE node, uniquely identified by the TE Router Address TLV. In this document the TE Router Address is referred to as the TE Router ID. The TE Router ID should not be confused with the OSPF Router ID, which uniquely identifies an OSPF router within an OSPF routing domain and is in a name space for control-plane components. The Router Address top-level TLV definition, processing and usage are largely unchanged; it specifies a stable OSPF TE node IP address, that is, the IP address is always reachable when there is IP connectivity to the associated OSPF TE node.

ASON defines a Routing Controller as an entity that handles the abstract information needed for routing and the routing information exchange with peering Routing Controllers, by operating on the Routing Database. It defines a Protocol Controller as an entity that handles protocol-specific message exchanges according to the reference point over which the information is exchanged, such as E-NNI and I-NNI, and internal exchanges with the Routing Controller. An OSPF router advertising ASON TE topology information performs both the functions of the Routing Controller and the Protocol Controller.
sections.plainLanguage: Two different numbers matter. The OSPF Router ID names the router as a protocol speaker. The TE Router ID names the optical node it speaks for, and one router may speak for several.

sections.title: Reachability and Link Attributes
sections.content:
In ASON, reachability information describes the set of endpoints that are reachable by the associated node in the transport plane. It represents transport-plane resources, such as an optical cross-connect interface, and uses transport-plane identifiers.

To advertise blocks of reachable address prefixes, a summarization mechanism is introduced that is based on the techniques described in RFC 5786. Blocks of reachable address prefixes are advertised together with the associated transport-plane node, which is identified in OSPF TE Link State Advertisements by its TE Router ID. The Node Attribute TLV defined in RFC 5786 is used to advertise the combination of a TE Router ID and its set of associated reachable address prefixes. It can contain a Local TE Router ID sub-TLV of length 4, a Node IPv4 Local Address sub-TLV and a Node IPv6 Local Address sub-TLV.

A router may support multiple transport nodes, and as a result may be required to advertise reachability separately for each transport node. It must therefore be possible for the router to originate more than one TE LSA containing the Node Attribute TLV. The Node Attribute TLV advertisement rules are relaxed accordingly: it may appear in more than one TE LSA originated by the Routing Controller when advertising reachability for a different transport node identified by the Local TE Router ID sub-TLV.

On link attributes, the mapping to OSPF TE Link TLV sub-TLVs is unchanged apart from local adaptation, which is defined as a link attribute that describes the cross- and inter-layer relationships. The Interface Switching Capability Descriptor identifies the ability of the TE link to support cross-connection to another link within the same layer, and, when advertising link adaptation, also the ability to use a locally terminated connection belonging to one layer as a data link for another layer. A link between two optical cross-connects contains at least one such attribute describing the Lambda Switching Capable capability. A link between an optical cross-connect and an IP/MPLS Label Switching Router contains at least two, one for the Lambda Switching Capable termination capability and one for the Packet Switching Capable adaptation capability. In OSPFv2 the descriptor is a sub-TLV of type 15 of the top-level Link TLV of type 2.
sections.plainLanguage: What gets advertised is reachability, meaning which addresses a given optical node can reach, and link attributes, meaning what a link can carry. The new part is that reachability has to be tied to a named optical node, because one router may look after several.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
For ASON routing, the control-plane component routing adjacency topology and the transport topology are not assumed to be congruent. Hence a single OSPF router must be able to advertise on behalf of multiple transport-layer nodes. The OSPF routers are identified by OSPF Router ID, and the transport nodes by TE Router ID.

The Router Address TLV is used to advertise the TE Router ID associated with the advertising Routing Controller. TE Router IDs for additional transport nodes are advertised through the Local and Remote TE Router ID sub-TLV and the Local TE Router ID sub-TLV. These Local TE Router Identifiers are typically used as the local endpoints for TE LSPs terminating on the associated transport node.

The Local and Remote TE Router ID sub-TLV is a new sub-TLV of the OSPFv2 TE LSA top-level Link TLV. Its Type field is 10 and its Length field is 8. The Value field contains 4 octets of the Local TE Router Identifier followed by 4 octets of the Remote TE Router Identifier, and neither may be zero. It must be included in the Link TLV if the OSPF router advertises on behalf of transport nodes with TE Router IDs different from the one in the Router Address TLV. If it is not included, or a value of 0 is given, the Link TLV will not be used for transport-plane path computation, and the condition should be logged for possible action by the network operator. When the sub-TLV is present it must be used to identify the local and remote transport node endpoints, and the Link-ID sub-TLV must be ignored and may be omitted.

The Local TE Router ID sub-TLV is a new sub-TLV of the top-level Node Attribute TLV. Its Type field is 5 and its Length field is 4, and the Value field contains the Local TE Router Identifier encoded over 4 octets. It must be included when the OSPF router advertises on behalf of transport nodes with TE Router IDs different from the one in the Router Address TLV. If it is not included, or a value of 0 is given, the Node Attribute TLV will not be used for determining ASON reachability.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new fields do the work. One sits inside a link advertisement and names the optical node at each end. The other sits inside a reachability advertisement and names the optical node that the addresses belong to.

sections.title: Dissemination and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
Routing Controllers supporting multiple routing areas disseminate information upward and downward in the ASON hierarchy by importing and exporting routing information as TE LSAs, which are area-scoped Opaque LSAs with Opaque type 1. The information that may be exchanged between adjacent levels includes the Router Address, Link and Node Attribute top-level TLVs. The imported and exported content may be transformed, for example filtered or aggregated, as long as the result is consistent. In practice, and to avoid scalability and processing overhead, routing information imported and exported in the hierarchy is expected to include reachability information and, under strict policy control, link topology information. These vertical dissemination mechanisms do not introduce or imply hierarchical OSPF areas.

When more than one Routing Controller is bound to an adjacent level of the ASON hierarchy and is configured to export routing information upward or downward, a mechanism is required to avoid looping. Looping is the re-advertisement of routing information into an RA that had previously advertised that information upward or downward. This could happen when the Routing Controller advertising downward is not the same one advertising upward.

The Inter-RA Export sub-TLVs prevent this. Type value 13 indicates that the associated routing information has been exported downward, and type value 12 indicates that it has been exported upward. Both sub-TLVs include the Routing Area ID from which the routing information was exported, which is not necessarily the RA that originated it but the RA from which it was immediately exported. The Length field takes the value 4 and the Value field contains the associated RA ID, which must be a unique identifier for the RA within the ASON routing domain.

TE LSAs may be imported or exported downward or upward, and the direction and advertising RA ID must be retained and advertised in the receiving RA. When exporting upward, any information received from a level above, tagged with an Inter-RA Export Downward sub-TLV, must not be exported upward; because an RA at Level N is contained by a single RA at Level N+1, this is the only checking needed and the RA ID is used solely for informational purposes. When exporting downward, any information received from a level below, tagged with an Inter-RA Export Upward sub-TLV, must not be exported downward if the target RA ID matches the RA ID associated with the routing information, because a single RA at Level N+1 may contain multiple RAs at Level N.
sections.plainLanguage: Information flows up the hierarchy and back down. Each advertisement carries a note saying which way it has already travelled and from which area, so that a receiving router can refuse to send it back where it came from.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.content:
The extensions described in the document are only applicable to ASON routing domains, and it is not expected that the attendant reachability and link information will ever be combined with global Internet or Layer 3 VPN routing. If there were ever a requirement for a given Routing Controller to participate in both domains, separate OSPFv2 instances would be used. In a multi-level ASON hierarchy, however, the potential volume of information could be quite large.

Routing information exchange upward and downward in the hierarchy between adjacent RAs must, by default, be limited to reachability information. In addition, several transformations such as prefix aggregation are recommended, to reduce the amount of information imported and exported by a given Routing Controller when such transformations will not impact consistency.

Routing information exchange involving traffic engineering attributes must be under strict policy control, and pacing and min/max thresholds for triggered updates are strongly recommended. The number of routing levels must be maintained under strict policy control.
sections.plainLanguage: Passing everything up and down a hierarchy of areas would be a lot of traffic, so the default is to pass only reachability, to summarise addresses where possible, and to keep the detailed link information under strict policy control.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document specifies the contents and processing of OSPFv2 TE LSAs. The TE LSA extensions defined in it are not used for Shortest Path First computation and have no direct effect on IP routing. ASON routing domains are also delimited by the usual administrative domain boundaries.

Any mechanisms used for securing the exchange of normal OSPF LSAs can be applied equally to all TE LSAs used in the ASON context. Authentication of OSPFv2 LSA exchanges, such as OSPF cryptographic authentication, can be used to provide significant protection against active attacks. RFC 5709 defines a mechanism for authenticating OSPFv2 packets by making use of the Hashed Message Authentication Code algorithm in conjunction with the SHA family of cryptographic hash functions.

Routing Controllers implementing export and import of ASON routing information between RAs must also include policy control of both the maximum amount of information advertised between RAs and the maximum rate at which it is advertised. This is to isolate the consequences of a Routing Controller being compromised to the RAs to which that subverted Routing Controller is attached.
sections.plainLanguage: These advertisements do not steer IP traffic, but they do describe the network. They should be authenticated like any other OSPF advertisement, and the amount of information passed between areas should be capped so that a compromised router cannot flood the hierarchy.

items.desc: Sub-TLV of the Node Attribute TLV. Length 4. Carries the TE Router ID of the transport node the advertised prefixes belong to.

items.desc: Sub-TLV of the Link TLV. Length 8. Carries the local and remote transport node endpoints of the link.

items.label: Inter-RA Export Upward
items.desc: Marks routing information as having been exported upward in the ASON hierarchy. Length 4, carrying the RA ID.

items.label: Inter-RA Export Downward
items.desc: Marks routing information as having been exported downward in the ASON hierarchy. Length 4, carrying the RA ID.

viz.caption: How routing information moves between levels, illustrative, not from the RFC

messages.label: Export upward
messages.note: Routing information is exported upward and tagged with the Inter-RA Export Upward sub-TLV carrying the RA ID.

messages.label: Export downward
messages.note: Information received from above must not be exported upward again; information received from below must not be sent back into that same RA.
